title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Publishing the Seventh Batch of Guiding Cases
ruling_gist_en: Where a person uses an information network to induce another person to click a false link, but actually steals property through a pre-installed computer program, constituting a crime, the person shall be convicted and punished for the crime of theft; where a person fabricates goods or services available for transaction, deceives another person into clicking a payment link, and thereby defrauds property, constituting a crime, the person shall be convicted and punished for the crime of fraud.
keywords_en: Criminal; Theft; Fraud; Using Information Networks
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Issuing the Seventh Batch of Guiding Cases

Fa [2014] No. 161

To the High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; and the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

Upon deliberation and approval by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, the following five cases (Guiding Cases No. 27-31), including the Zang Jinquan et al. case of theft and fraud, are hereby issued as the seventh batch of guiding cases for reference in adjudicating similar cases.

June 26, 2014

Guiding Case No. 27

Zang Jinquan et al. v. — dispute over theft and fraud

(Deliberated and approved by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on June 23, 2014)

Keywords: criminal, theft, fraud, use of information network

Ruling Gist

Where an actor, using an information network, induces another person to click on a false link but actually steals property through a pre-installed computer program, thereby constituting a crime, the actor shall be convicted and punished for the crime of theft; where an actor fabricates commodities or services available for transaction, deceives another person into clicking on a payment link for the purpose of defrauding property, thereby constituting a crime, the actor shall be convicted and punished for the crime of fraud.

Related Legal Provisions

Article 264 and Article 266 of the Criminal Law of the PRC

Basic Facts

I. Facts of Theft

On June 1, 2010, after defrauding the victim, Jin, of RMB 195, the defendant Zheng Biling learned that Jin's online banking account with China Construction Bank contained more than RMB 305,000 in deposits with no daily payment limit, and then informed the defendant Zang Jinquan of this by telephone, planning to commit the crime jointly. Zang Jinquan went to an internet cafe, and on the pretext that he had not yet seen the record of Jin's successful payment, sent Jin a false link marked with a transaction amount of RMB 1 but actually embedded with a computer program to pay RMB 305,000, falsely claiming that after Jin clicked on the RMB 1 payment link, Zang would be able to view the successful payment record. Induced, Jin clicked on the false link, and the RMB 305,000 in his online banking account with China Construction Bank was immediately transferred, through the computer program preset by Zang Jinquan, via the platform of Shanghai Kuaiqian Information Service Co., Ltd., to the account "kissal23" that Zang Jinquan had previously registered with Fuzhou Haidu Sunshine Information Technology Co., Ltd. Zang Jinquan used RMB 116,863 of this amount to purchase a large quantity of game point cards, and then sold them for cash on his Taobao store "Xiaoquan Xiansheng Oh." After the case was discovered, the public security organs recovered RMB 187,126.31 in stolen funds and returned them to the victim.

II. Facts of Fraud

Between May and June 2010, the defendants Zang Jinquan, Zheng Biling, and Liu Tao each opened Taobao stores under false identities, offering no actual goods for sale, and attracted buyers with low prices. The three defendants first registered an account on an online game website and preset a recharge procedure for that account, with the recharge amount being the amount the buyer intended to pay, and then embedded the code for this recharge procedure into a false Taobao link. After negotiating the price of the goods with the buyer, each of the three defendants sent the false Taobao link to the buyer through the Aliwangwang chat tool, on the pretext of facilitating the buyer's purchase. The buyer, mistakenly believing it to be a Taobao link, clicked on the link to conduct the purchase and payment, and thought that the payment would be remitted to the public account set up by Alipay for secured transactions, but the payment was actually transferred through the preset procedure to the private account of the online game website at Alipay, and then to the recharge account that the defendants had previously registered on the online game website. After obtaining the buyer's payment, the three defendants purchased game point cards, Tencent Q coins, etc., on the online game website, and then, according to their prior agreement, uniformly placed them for sale on Zang Jinquan's Taobao store "Xiaoquan Xiansheng Oh" to obtain cash. The proceeds were all remitted to Zang Jinquan's ICBC card, and Zang distributed them according to the agreed method based on the amount of profit.

After pre-conspiring, the defendants Zang Jinquan, Zheng Biling, and Liu Tao successively went to internet cafes in Suzhou, Wuxi, Kunshan and other places in Jiangsu Province to commit the crimes using the above methods. Zang Jinquan defrauded RMB 22,000 and profited over RMB 5,000; Zheng Biling profited over RMB 5,000; and Liu Tao profited over RMB 12,000.

Judgment

The Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court of Zhejiang Province, on June 1, 2011, rendered criminal judgment (2011) Zhe Hang Xing Chu Zi No. 91: 1. The defendant Zang Jinquan was convicted of theft and sentenced to 13 years' imprisonment, deprived of political rights for 1 year, and fined RMB 30,000; he was convicted of fraud and sentenced to 2 years' imprisonment and fined RMB 5,000; the combined sentence was fixed at 14 years and 6 months' imprisonment, deprivation of political rights for 1 year, and a fine of RMB 35,000. 2. The defendant Zheng Biling was convicted of theft and sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment, deprived of political rights for 1 year, and fined RMB 10,000; she was convicted of fraud and sentenced to 6 months' imprisonment and fined RMB 2,000; the combined sentence was fixed at 10 years and 3 months' imprisonment, deprivation of political rights for 1 year, and a fine of RMB 12,000. 3. The defendant Liu Tao was convicted of fraud and sentenced to 1 year and 6 months' imprisonment and fined RMB 5,000. After the judgment was pronounced, Zang Jinquan appealed. The Zhejiang High People's Court, on August 9, 2011, rendered criminal ruling (2011) Zhe Xing San Zhong Zi No. 132, rejecting the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held: Theft is the act of secretly stealing public or private property for the purpose of illegal possession; fraud is the act of obtaining public or private property by deception, using fabricated facts or concealing the truth, for the purpose of illegal possession. Where an act of illegally possessing property involves both secret stealing and deceptive means, the distinction between theft and fraud should be made based on the main means used by the actor and whether the victim had the awareness of disposing of property. If the decisive means by which the actor obtains property is secret stealing, and the deceptive act merely creates conditions or provides cover for the theft, and the victim did not "voluntarily" deliver the property, it should be characterized as theft; if the decisive means by which the actor obtains property is deception, and the victim "voluntarily" delivers the property based on a mistaken understanding, and theft is merely an auxiliary means, it should be characterized as fraud. In the context of information networks, where an actor uses an information network to induce another person to click on a false link but actually steals property through a pre-installed computer program, thereby constituting a crime, the actor should be convicted and punished for the crime of theft; where an actor fabricates commodities or services available for transaction, deceives another person into clicking on a payment link for the purpose of paying for goods, and thereby obtains property, constituting a crime, the actor should be convicted and punished for the crime of fraud. In this case, the defendants Zang Jinquan and Zheng Biling used the method of pre-designing and embedding a computer program to secretly steal a large amount of money from another person's online banking account, and their acts both constituted the crime of theft. Zang Jinquan, Zheng Biling, and the defendant Liu Tao, for the purpose of illegal possession, deceived others into paying a relatively large amount of money for goods by opening false online stores and using forged shopping links, and their acts all constituted the crime of fraud. Zang and Zheng should be punished for multiple crimes in accordance with the law.

Regarding the defense and arguments raised by the defendant Zang Jinquan and his defense counsel that the act of illegally obtaining RMB 305,000 from the victim Jin's online banking account did not constitute theft but rather fraud, the court found, upon investigation, that after Zang Jinquan and the defendant Zheng Biling learned that Jin's online banking account contained funds, they immediately formed the intent to illegally possess the funds by embedding a computer program; thereafter, during online chat, they induced Jin to agree to pay RMB 1, while actually creating a false Taobao link that appeared to pay "RMB 1" but actually paid RMB 305,000, causing Jin, after clicking, to have RMB 305,000 in his online banking account illegally transferred to Zang Jinquan's registered account, of which Jin was unaware and to which he did not consent. It is evident that the decisive means by which Zang and Zheng obtained the property was secret stealing; inducing the victim to click on the false "RMB 1" link was an auxiliary means of implementing the theft, merely creating conditions or providing cover for the theft, and the victim did not "voluntarily" deliver the substantial amount of money. The obtaining of the bank deposit was actually accomplished by secretly stealing through the hidden, pre-installed computer program, which conforms to the constitutive elements of the crime of theft. In accordance with Articles 264 and 287 of the Criminal Law, the act should be convicted and punished as theft. Therefore, the above defenses and arguments raised by Zang Jinquan and his defense counsel were inconsistent with the facts and legal provisions and were not adopted.

Guiding Case No. 28

Hu Kejin v. — dispute over refusal to pay labor remuneration

(Deliberated and approved by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on June 23, 2014)

Keywords: criminal, crime of refusing to pay labor remuneration, unit or individual lacking qualification for employing workers

Ruling Gist

1. Where a unit or individual (contractor) lacking the qualification to employ workers employs workers illegally and refuses to pay their labor remuneration, and the amount is relatively large, and payment is still refused after being ordered by the relevant government department, criminal liability for the crime of refusing to pay labor remuneration shall be pursued.

2. Where a unit or individual (contractor) lacking the qualification to employ workers refuses to pay labor remuneration, even if another unit or individual advances the labor remuneration before criminal filing, this does not affect the pursuit of criminal liability of the employing unit or individual (contractor) for the crime of refusing to pay labor remuneration.

Related Legal Provisions

Paragraph 1, Article 276a of the Criminal Law of the PRC

Basic Facts

In December 2010, the defendant Hu Kejin subcontracted part of the landscape engineering for Phase I of Sansheng Feilishan, located in Huangshui Town, Shuangliu County, Sichuan Province, and then employed multiple migrant workers to enter the site for construction. During the construction period, Hu Kejin received a total of over RMB 510,000 in project payments from the employer, which exceeded the actual project cost confirmed at the time of settlement. After the project was completed on June 5, 2011, Hu Kejin, citing project losses, owed over RMB 120,000 in wages to more than 20 migrant workers, including Li Chaowen. On June 9, the Shuangliu County Human Resources and Social Security Bureau ordered Hu Kejin to pay the outstanding wages. However, Hu booked a flight ticket that evening and fled by plane the next morning. On June 30, Sichuan Jintianxia Landscape Engineering Co., Ltd., as the general contractor of the project, advanced over RMB 120,000 on behalf of Hu Kejin to pay the wages of the migrant workers. On July 4, the public security organs filed a criminal case for Hu Kejin's refusal to pay labor remuneration. On July 12, Hu Kejin was arrested in Cixi City, Zhejiang Province.

Judgment

The Shuangliu County People's Court of Sichuan Province, on December 29, 2011, rendered criminal judgment (2011) Shuangliu Xing Chu Zi No. 544, finding the defendant Hu Kejin guilty of the crime of refusing to pay labor remuneration, sentencing him to one year's imprisonment, and imposing a fine of RMB 20,000. After the judgment was pronounced, the defendant did not appeal, and the judgment became legally effective.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held: The defendant Hu Kejin refused to pay over RMB 120,000 in labor remuneration to more than 20 migrant workers, a relatively large amount, and fled after being ordered by the relevant government department to pay, and his act constituted the crime of refusing to pay labor remuneration. Although the defendant Hu Kejin did not have legal employment qualifications, lacked the corresponding qualifications for construction projects in undertaking the construction project, and illegally employed migrant workers for construction, these circumstances do not affect the pursuit of criminal liability for the crime of refusing to pay labor remuneration. In this case, after Hu Kejin fled, the general contractor, in accordance with relevant regulations, settled the wages owed by Hu to the migrant workers. This act of settling the overdue wages constituted an advance on behalf of Hu. Although this act mitigated the social harm of the default, it did not exempt Hu from the obligation to pay labor remuneration. Therefore, Hu Kejin's criminal liability for the crime of refusing to pay labor remuneration should still be pursued. In view of the fact that Hu Kejin was a first-time offender and had a good attitude of admission of guilt, the above judgment was rendered in accordance with the law.

Guiding Case No. 29

Tianjin China Youth Travel Service v. Tianjin Guoqing International Travel Service Co., Ltd. — dispute over unauthorized use of another's enterprise name

(Deliberated and approved by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on June 26, 2014)

Keywords: civil, unfair competition, unauthorized use of another's enterprise name

Ruling Gist

1. An abbreviation of an enterprise name that has been used by the enterprise for a long period and extensively externally, has a certain degree of market recognition and is known to the relevant public, and has actually functioned as a trade name, may be regarded as an enterprise name and protected accordingly.

2. Unauthorized use of another's enterprise name abbreviation that has actually functioned as a trade name as a keyword for internet pay-per-click advertising in commercial activities, causing confusion or mistaken belief among the relevant public, constitutes an act of unfair competition.

Related Legal Provisions

1. Article 120 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC

2. Article 5 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the PRC

Basic Facts

The plaintiff, Tianjin China Youth Travel Service (hereinafter referred to as Tianjin CYTS), alleged: The defendant, Tianjin Guoqing International Travel Service Co., Ltd., illegally used the plaintiff's full enterprise name and its abbreviation "Tianjin Qinglv" on its copyright-owned website pages, website source code, and search engines, in violation of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. The plaintiff requested the court to order the defendant to immediately cease the unfair competition act, make a public apology, compensate for economic losses of RMB 100,000, and bear the litigation costs.

The defendant, Tianjin Guoqing International Travel Service Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tianjin Guoqing Travel), argued: "Tianjin Qinglv" was not registered and was not owned by the plaintiff. The plaintiff's claimed losses lacked a factual and legal basis. The defendant requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

The court found through trial: Tianjin China Youth Travel Service was established on November 1, 1986, and was a state-owned enterprise engaged in domestic and inbound/outbound travel services, directly under the Communist Youth League Tianjin Municipal Committee. The Communist Youth League Tianjin Municipal Committee issued a certificate stating that "Tianjin Qinglv" is the abbreviation of Tianjin China Youth Travel Service. Beginning in 2007, media such as Jinwan Bao started to refer to Tianjin China Youth Travel Service by the abbreviation "Tianjin Qinglv" in reports of activities organized by Tianjin CYTS. Tianjin CYTS used "Tianjin Qinglv" as its abbreviation in daily business activities, including in quotations, travel contracts, cooperation documents with peers in the industry, invoices, and on store signs at various business locations. Tianjin Guoqing International Travel Service Co., Ltd. was established on July 6, 2010, and was a limited liability company engaged in domestic travel and inbound travel reception services.

At the end of 2010, Tianjin CYTS discovered that when searching for "Tianjin China Youth Travel Service" or "Tianjin Qinglv" on the Google search engine, the first search result, marked as a sponsored link, displayed "Tianjin China Youth Travel Service Online Business Hall www.lechuou.com Tianjin Guoqing Online Business Hall, your ideal choice, providing quality, caring, and comfortable services for your trip" or "Tianjin Qinglv Online Business Hall www.lechuou.com Tianjin Guoqing Online Business Hall, your ideal choice, providing quality, caring, and comfortable services for your trip." Clicking on the link led to a website labeled as Tianjin Guoqing International Travel Service's "Le Chu You" website. At the top of the page appeared words such as "Tianjin Guoqing International Travel Service - Qingnian Travel Service Qinglv/Tianjin Guo Travel." The content of the webpage consisted of information and quotations for Tianjin Guoqing Travel's tourism business. The website was marked as copyright owned by: "Le Chu You - Tianjin Guoqing," and displayed Tianjin Guoqing's contact number and business address. At the same time, when searching for "Tianjin Qinglv" on the Baidu search engine, the first search result, marked as a promoted link, displayed "Welcome to Tianjin Qinglv, an enterprise that values contracts and honors commitments, featuring classic domestic and outbound travel itineraries, 100% group departures, Tianjin Qinglv 400-611-5253 022.ctsg.cn." Clicking on the link led to the same website labeled as Tianjin Guoqing's "Le Chu You" website.

Judgment

Tianjin Second Intermediate People's Court, on October 24, 2011, rendered civil judgment (2011) Er Zhong Min San Zhi Chu Zi No. 135: 1. The defendant, Tianjin Guoqing International Travel Service Co., Ltd., shall immediately cease the infringing act; 2. The defendant shall, within thirty days of the judgment taking effect, post an apology statement on its company website for a period of 15 days; 3. The defendant shall compensate the plaintiff, Tianjin China Youth Travel Service, for economic losses of RMB 30,000; 4. The plaintiff's other claims are dismissed. After the judgment was pronounced, Tianjin Guoqing Travel appealed. The Tianjin High People's Court, on March 20, 2012, rendered civil judgment (2012) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 3: 1. Affirmed items 2, 3, and 4 of the above civil judgment of Tianjin Second Intermediate People's Court; 2. Modified item 1 of the judgment, changing "The defendant, Tianjin Guoqing International Travel Service Co., Ltd., shall immediately cease the infringing act" to "The defendant, Tianjin Guoqing International Travel Service Co., Ltd., shall immediately cease using the words 'Tianjin China Youth Travel Service' and 'Tianjin Qinglv' and using them as search link keywords for the website of Tianjin Guoqing International Travel Service Co., Ltd."; 3. Dismissed the defendant's other appeal claims.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held: According to paragraph 1 of Article 6 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Cases of Unfair Competition, "The enterprise name registered with the enterprise registration authority in accordance with the law, as well as the name of a foreign (regional) enterprise used for commercial purposes within the territory of China, shall be deemed as the 'enterprise name' as stipulated in Item (3) of Article 5 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. The core part of the enterprise name that has a certain degree of market recognition and is known to the relevant public may be deemed as the 'enterprise name' as stipulated in Item (3) of Article 5 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law." Therefore, an abbreviation of an enterprise name that has been used by the enterprise for a long period and extensively externally, has a certain degree of market recognition and is known to the relevant public, and has actually functioned as a trade name, should also be regarded as an enterprise name and protected accordingly. "Tianjin China Youth Travel Service" is the enterprise name that the plaintiff has used since its establishment in 1986, and the plaintiff enjoys the exclusive right to that enterprise name. "Tianjin Qinglv," as the abbreviation of that enterprise name, had been widely used by the plaintiff in business activities since 2007, and relevant media reports and customers also used "Tianjin Qinglv" to refer to Tianjin China Youth Travel Service. Through years of use and publicity in business activities, it had acquired a certain degree of market recognition, become known to the relevant public, and established a stable association with Tianjin China Youth Travel Service, thus functioning as a business identifier capable of indicating the business operator. Therefore, "Tianjin Qinglv" can be regarded as an enterprise name and protected together with "Tianjin China Youth Travel Service."

Article 5(3) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China provides that business operators shall not engage in market transactions by improper means such as using the enterprise name of others without authorization to cause others to mistake their goods for those of others, thereby harming competitors. Therefore, where a business operator, without authorization, uses another person's enterprise name or abbreviation as a keyword for internet paid ranking, causing public confusion and mistake, and exploits the other's popularity and goodwill to achieve the purpose of promoting itself, such conduct constitutes an act of unfair competition and shall be prohibited. Tianjin Guoqinglv, as a business operator engaged in tourism services, without the permission of Tianjin Qinglv, by setting keywords related to the enterprise name of Tianjin Qinglv in relevant search engines and using them in the website source code, caused the relevant public, when searching the keywords "Tianjin China Youth Travel Service" and "Tianjin Qinglv," to directly display the website link of Tianjin Guoqinglv, thereby entering the website of Tianjin Guoqinglv to contact for tourism business, achieving the effect of using the initial confusion of network users to seize potential customers. Subjectively, it had the intent to cause mistake or confusion among the relevant public during online searches and inquiries; objectively, it used "Tianjin China Youth Travel Service" and "Tianjin Qinglv" without authorization, exploiting the business reputation of Tianjin Qinglv, damaging the legitimate rights and interests of Tianjin Qinglv. Its conduct constitutes an act of unfair competition and shall be prohibited by law. Tianjin Guoqinglv, as a competitor in the same industry as Tianjin Qinglv, knowing that the enterprise name and abbreviation of Tianjin Qinglv enjoyed high popularity, still used them without authorization, having the intention to seek improper benefits by borrowing another's name, with obvious subjective malice. In accordance with Article 120 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, Tianjin Guoqinglv shall bear the legal liability of ceasing the infringement, eliminating the effects, and compensating for losses. As for the words "Youth Travel Service Qinglv" displayed at the top of the webpage of Tianjin Guoqinglv, they are not within the scope of protection of the plaintiff's enterprise name and do not constitute unfair competition against the plaintiff.

Guiding Case No. 30

Lan Jianjun and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Technology Co., Ltd. v. Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Service Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over infringement of trademark rights and unfair competition

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on June 26, 2014)

Keywords: civil, infringement of trademark rights, unfair competition, competitive relationship

Ruling Gist

1. Whether a business operator has acted beyond its legally approved scope of business and violated laws and regulations on administrative licensing does not affect its exercise of civil rights to stop trademark infringement and unfair competition in accordance with the law.

2. The Anti-Unfair Competition Law does not restrict that a direct competitive relationship must exist between business operators, nor does it require them to engage in the same industry. Where there is an indirect competitive relationship between business operators, and the actor violates the provisions of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law and damages the legitimate rights and interests of other business operators, the conduct shall also be deemed as unfair competition.

Related Legal Provisions

Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Plaintiffs Lan Jianjun and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi) alleged: They lawfully enjoyed the exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Xiaomuzhi," and Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Service Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tianjin Xiaomuzhi) and Tianjin Huashang Automobile Import Parts Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tianjin Huashang), in the course of engaging in automobile maintenance and soliciting franchisees through their websites, used the "" mark in many places, and separately or prominently used the term "Xiaomuzhi," thereby infringing their exclusive right to use the registered trademark. Moreover, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi used the prior enterprise name of Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi without authorization, constituting unfair competition against Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi. Therefore, they requested the court to order Tianjin Xiaomuzhi to immediately cease using the trade name "Xiaomuzhi" in its business, order Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang to cease the acts of trademark infringement and unfair competition, make a public apology, jointly and severally compensate for economic losses of RMB 630,000 and reasonable expenses of RMB 24,379.4, and bear the litigation costs of the case.

Defendants Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang argued: 1. The scope of business of Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi did not include licensed items or automobile maintenance services, nor did it obtain the license for motor vehicle maintenance, and it did not meet the "two stores, one year" conditions for franchising; thus its operations were illegal beyond the scope of business, and its rights should not be protected. 2. Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang had a legitimate source for using the "Xiaomuzhi" mark and did not constitute trademark infringement. 3. Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi was not engaged in the automobile maintenance industry; thus there was no commercial competitive relationship between the parties. Moreover, it failed to prove that it was a well-known enterprise, and its claim for the right to an enterprise name lacked legal basis. Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang did not constitute unfair competition, and therefore requested the court to reject the plaintiffs' claims.

The court found through trial: Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi was established on October 22, 2004, with its legal representative being Lan Jianjun. Its scope of business was: "Licensed items: none; General business items: services: technical development of automobile glass repair, technical development of quick automobile paint repair; wholesale and retail: automobile parts; including the scope of business of its subordinate branches; all other lawful projects not requiring approval (the above scope of business does not include items prohibited, restricted, or requiring licensing by state laws and regulations). For items involving the licensing system, operation shall be based on the license." Its subordinate branch was Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Xiaoshan Branch, established on November 8, 2005, with the scope of business: "Automobile painting, glass installation." The "Road Transport Business License" obtained by this branch on August 1, 2008, indicated the scope of business as: "Maintenance (Class II motor vehicle maintenance: small vehicle maintenance)."

On January 14, 2011, Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi obtained the registered trademark No. 6573882 for the word mark "Xiaomuzhi," with approved services (Class 35): chain store management (commercial administration assistance); commercial management of franchised operations; commercial management consulting; advertising (cut-off). The trademark is currently within its validity period. On April 14, 2011, Lan Jianjun granted Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi an exclusive license to use the registered trademark No. 6573881 for the word mark "Xiaomuzhi" owned by him.

Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi has been awarded the China Franchise Chain Top 120 certificate multiple times by the China Chain Store and Franchise Association. In 2009, the "Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Service" of Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi was recognized as a Zhejiang Service Brand by the Zhejiang Provincial Bureau of Quality and Technical Supervision.

Tianjin Xiaomuzhi was established on October 16, 2008, with its legal representative being Tian Junshan. Its scope of business was: "Complete overhaul of small passenger cars, overhaul of assemblies, complete vehicle maintenance, minor repairs, repair and rescue, special repairs. (The operation period of licensed items is subject to the license)." The "Tianjin Motor Vehicle Maintenance Operation License" obtained by the company on July 28, 2010, indicated the category as "Class II (Automobile Maintenance)" and the operation items as "Complete overhaul of small passenger cars, overhaul of assemblies, complete vehicle maintenance, minor repairs, repair and rescue, special repairs." The validity period was from July 28, 2010 to July 27, 2012.

Tianjin Huashang was established on November 23, 1992, with the same legal representative as Tianjin Xiaomuzhi, i.e., Tian Junshan. Its scope of business was: "Automobile parts, glass, lubricating grease, tires, automobile accessories; body cleaning and maintenance, electrical system repair, painting; express delivery, consignment, information consulting; general cargo (the above scope of business items requiring industry licenses shall operate within the validity period of the license, and matters with special state regulations shall be handled accordingly)." The "Tianjin Motor Vehicle Maintenance Operation License" obtained by Tianjin Huashang indicated the operation items as: "Complete overhaul of small passenger cars, overhaul of assemblies, complete vehicle maintenance, minor repairs, repair and rescue, special repairs," with the category as Class II (Automobile Maintenance), and is currently within the validity period.

Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang, in the course of engaging in automobile maintenance and soliciting franchisees through their websites, used the "" mark in many places, and separately or prominently used the term "Xiaomuzhi."

On June 30, 2008, Tianjin Huashang and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi entered into a "Franchised Chain Operation Contract," granting Tianjin Huashang the right to operate a "Xiaomuzhi" brand automobile maintenance chain center in Tianjin, with the contract term from June 30, 2008 to June 29, 2011. Article 3(4) of the contract stipulated: "Party B (Tianjin Huashang) shall establish franchised stores and conduct business activities using the name approved in writing by Party A (Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi). Restrictions on the use of trade names (choose one to use): (√) Without the written consent of Party A, Party B shall not use or register the 'Xiaomuzhi' or 'Xiaomuzhi Micro-Repair' or related marks as an enterprise name registration at any time or in any place or in any form; without the written consent of Party A, Party B shall not add any prefix or suffix to modify or supplement the name 'Xiaomuzhi' or 'Xiaomuzhi Micro-Repair'; Party B shall not register a domain name containing 'Xiaomuzhi' or 'Xiaomuzhi Micro-Repair' or any related or similar characters, and this restriction includes restrictions on Party B's branches." On December 16, 2010, a dispute arose between Tianjin Huashang and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi regarding the performance of the "Franchised Chain Operation Contract," and the Hangzhou Arbitration Commission ruled to terminate the contract by arbitration.

It was also found that Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi obtained the commercial franchising record-filing from the Ministry of Commerce on April 8, 2008. Tianjin Huashang once reported to the competent administrative department of the Ministry of Commerce that Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi was engaging in franchising activities in violation of regulations and that its record-filing should be revoked. In response, the Zhejiang Provincial Department of Commerce issued a letter titled "Report on the Franchising Situation of Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Technology Co., Ltd.," which recorded: 1. At the time of record-filing for commercial franchising, Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi had already met the "two stores, one year" condition, in compliance with Article 7 of the "Regulations on the Administration of Commercial Franchising," and could be filed; 2. Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi was mainly responsible for the management of the "Xiaomuzhi" brand and did not directly engage in motor vehicle maintenance business, and it had its own trademarks, patents, business models, and other business resources, allowing it to carry out franchising business; 3. According to inquiries with the relevant person in charge of the Zhejiang Provincial Road Transport Administration, the directly operated stores of Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi held "Road Transport Business Licenses" with a scope of business including "Class III motor vehicle maintenance" or "Class II motor vehicle maintenance," and had the qualifications to engage in motor vehicle maintenance; 4. The authorization and licensing of Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi, as well as motor vehicle maintenance operations, were not within the scope of franchising permits.

Judgment

The Tianjin Second Intermediate People's Court rendered the civil judgment (2012) Er Zhong Min San Zhi Chu Zi No. 47 on September 17, 2012:

1. As of the effective date of this judgment, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Service Co., Ltd. shall immediately cease the acts of infringing the registered trademarks Nos. 6573881 and 6573882 for the word mark "Xiaomuzhi," i.e., Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Service Co., Ltd. shall immediately cease using the "" mark and shall cease using the term "Xiaomuzhi" separately on its website (www.txiaomuhi.net), promotional materials, discount experience coupons, and its business premises (including branches); 2. As of the effective date of this judgment, Tianjin Huashang Automobile Import Parts Co., Ltd. shall immediately cease the acts of infringing the registered trademarks Nos. 6573881 and 6573882 for the word mark "Xiaomuzhi," i.e., Tianjin Huashang Automobile Import Parts Co., Ltd. shall immediately cease using the "" mark on its website (www.txiaomuzhi.com); 3. Within ten days of the effective date of this judgment, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Service Co., Ltd. and Tianjin Huashang Automobile Import Parts Co., Ltd. shall jointly and severally compensate Lan Jianjun and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Technology Co., Ltd. for economic losses and rights enforcement expenses totaling RMB 50,000; 4. The other claims of Lan Jianjun and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Technology Co., Ltd. are rejected. After the judgment was pronounced, Lan Jianjun, Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi, and Tianjin Huashang all appealed. The Tianjin High People's Court rendered the civil judgment (2012) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 0046 on February 19, 2013: 1. Affirmed items 1, 2, and 3 of the civil judgment (2012) Er Zhong Min San Zhi Chu Zi No. 47 of the Tianjin Second Intermediate People's Court and the part concerning liability for overdue performance; 2. Reversed item 4 of the civil judgment (2012) Er Zhong Min San Zhi Chu Zi No. 47 of the Tianjin Second Intermediate People's Court; 3. As of the effective date of this judgment, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Service Co., Ltd. shall immediately cease using the trade name "Xiaomuzhi" in its enterprise name; 4. Within ten days of the effective date of this judgment, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Service Co., Ltd. shall compensate Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Technology Co., Ltd. for economic losses of RMB 30,000; 5. The other appeal claims of Lan Jianjun and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Technology Co., Ltd. are rejected; 6. The appeal claims of Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Automobile Maintenance Service Co., Ltd. and Tianjin Huashang Automobile Import Parts Co., Ltd. are rejected.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: The main issues in dispute in this case were whether the alleged infringing acts of the defendants, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang, infringed the exclusive right to use the registered trademarks of the plaintiffs, Lan Jianjun and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi, and whether they constituted unfair competition against Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi.

I. Whether the defendants infringed the exclusive right to use the registered trademarks of Lan Jianjun and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi

Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang, in the course of engaging in automobile maintenance and soliciting franchisees through their websites, used the "" mark in many places, and separately or prominently used the term "Xiaomuzhi." The relevant public, applying ordinary attention, would be sufficiently likely to be confused as to the source of the services or to mistakenly believe that there was a specific connection between Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi. The main and most easily identifiable part of the "" mark, the term "Xiaomuzhi," is identical to the registered trademark in question. Considering also the trademark use of "Xiaomuzhi" by Tianjin Xiaomuzhi at its business premises, on its website, and in promotional materials, it should be determined that this mark is similar to the registered word trademark "Xiaomuzhi" in question. Accordingly, since Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang, without permission, used the "" mark and separately used the term "Xiaomuzhi" in services identical to those approved for the registered trademark No. 6573881 for the word mark "Xiaomuzhi" owned by Lan Jianjun and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi, which was sufficient to cause confusion or mistake among the relevant public, this constituted the infringement act specified in Article 52(1) of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Law). Regarding the commercial acts of Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang in soliciting franchisees through their websites, in accordance with Article 12 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Civil Disputes over Trademarks, it can be determined that similar trademarks were used in services similar to those approved for the registered trademark No. 6573882 for the word mark "Xiaomuzhi" owned by Lan Jianjun and Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi, and without the permission of the right holder, this also constituted the infringement act specified in Article 52(1) of the Trademark Law.

II. Whether the defendants constituted unfair competition against Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi

This disputed issue involves two key questions: First, whether the business operator had acted beyond its legally approved scope of business in violation of laws and regulations on administrative licensing and whether its civil rights and interests can be protected by law; Second, how to determine the competitive relationship regulated by the Anti-Unfair Competition Law.

(1) Whether the business operator had acted beyond its legally approved scope of business and whether its civil rights and interests can be protected by law

A main reason argued by Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang that their conduct did not constitute unfair competition was that Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi had not obtained the relevant license for motor vehicle maintenance, had acted beyond its legally approved scope of business to engage in franchising and did not meet the legal conditions, thus engaging in illegal operations. Therefore, the civil rights and interests claimed by Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi should not be protected by law. Accordingly, in this case, it must be clarified whether the conduct alleged by Tianjin Xiaomuzhi and Tianjin Huashang that Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi had acted beyond its legally approved scope of business in violation of laws and regulations on administrative licensing was established, and whether the corresponding civil rights and interests could be protected by law.

First, conduct that exceeds the legally approved scope of business and violates relevant laws and regulations on administrative licensing should be determined by the corresponding administrative department in accordance with the law. The party claiming that the other party has engaged in illegal business operations shall bear the corresponding burden of proof. In this case, regarding whether Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi had engaged in illegal motor vehicle maintenance and franchising business, based on the existing evidence and facts, it was difficult to reach an affirmative conclusion. Operating automobile maintenance is a project subject to licensing by law, but Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi did not engage in automobile maintenance business; what it actually did was authorize others to use its trademark in services such as vehicle cleaning, maintenance, and repair, or license its directly operated stores and franchisees to use its "Xiaomuzhi" brand, patented technology, etc., in their business activities through commercial franchising. This did not require its own acquisition of a license for motor vehicle maintenance business as a prerequisite. Furthermore, Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi had obtained commercial franchising record-filing from the Ministry of Commerce. At the time of record-filing for commercial franchising, it had already met the "two stores, one year" condition. It was mainly responsible for the management of the "Xiaomuzhi" brand, did not directly engage in motor vehicle maintenance business, and had its own trademarks, patents, business models, and other business resources, allowing it to carry out franchising business. Therefore, based on the existing evidence, it could not be determined that Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi had engaged in motor vehicle maintenance or franchising business in violation of laws and regulations on administrative licensing.

Second, even if the relevant conduct exceeded the legally approved scope of business and violated laws and regulations on administrative licensing, it should be investigated and dealt with by the administrative department in accordance with the law. This does not necessarily affect the qualification of a party whose civil rights and interests are infringed to file a civil lawsuit, nor can it serve as a defense for the alleged infringer that its conduct does not constitute infringement. In this case, even if Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi had acted beyond its legally approved scope of business and violated laws and regulations on administrative licensing, this falls within the scope of administrative liability. Such conduct does not affect its exercise of civil rights to stop trademark infringement and unfair competition in accordance with the law, nor does it affect the people's court's protection of its civil rights and interests in accordance with the law. Where the alleged infringer claims that its conduct does not constitute infringement on the ground that the business operator has acted beyond its legally approved scope of business and violated laws and regulations on administrative licensing, the people's court shall not support such a claim.

(2) How to determine the competitive relationship regulated by the Anti-Unfair Competition Law

Whether there is a competitive relationship between business operators is the key to determining the constitution of unfair competition. Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Anti-Unfair Competition Law) stipulates: "Business operators shall, in their market transactions, follow the principles of voluntariness, equality, fairness, honesty and creditworthiness, and abide by generally recognized commercial ethics. Unfair competition as mentioned in this Law refers to acts that violate the provisions of this Law, impair the lawful rights and interests of other business operators, and disrupt the order of the social economy. Business operators as mentioned in this Law refer to legal persons, other economic organizations, and individuals engaged in the production or sale of commodities or the provision of profitable services (hereinafter commodities include services)." It can be seen that the Anti-Unfair Competition Law does not limit the requirement that there must be a direct or specific competitive relationship between business operators, nor does it require that business operators engage in the same industry. The unfair competition acts regulated by the Anti-Unfair Competition Law refer to acts that harm the lawful rights and interests of other business operators and disrupt the economic order. From the perspective of the direct object of harm, what is harmed is the market interests of other business operators. Therefore, if business operators have an indirect competitive relationship and the actor violates the provisions of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, harming the lawful rights and interests of other business operators, it should also be deemed as an act of unfair competition.

In this case, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company and Tianjin Huashang Company, which are alleged to have engaged in unfair competition, are both engaged in the automotive repair industry. According to the facts found, Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company does not itself possess the qualifications to engage in motor vehicle repair and has not actually engaged in automotive repair business. However, based on its technical development activities such as automotive glass repair and rapid automotive paint repair, as well as the vehicle maintenance and repair services included in the registered trademark service items licensed for use, it can be determined that Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company, by licensing its enterprise logo, registered trademark, patents, proprietary technology, and other business resources to its directly operated stores or franchise stores, operates as a "Xiaomuzhi" brand operator, engaging in business activities related to automotive repair through commercial franchising. Therefore, Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company is a relevant operator in the automotive repair market, and there is an indirect competitive relationship between it and Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company and Tianjin Huashang Company.

Article 5, item (3) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law prohibits business operators from misappropriating the enterprise names of others, leading people to mistake them as the goods of others, thereby harming competitors. On the basis of determining that the plaintiff and the defendant have an indirect competitive relationship, determining whether Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company's registration of "Xiaomuzhi" as its trade name constitutes the act of misappropriating another's enterprise name as unfair competition requires comprehensive consideration of the following factors:

1. Whether the enterprise name of Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company has a certain degree of market recognition. Based on the existing evidence in this case, Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company has used "Xiaomuzhi" as its trade name since its establishment in October 2004, engaged in the automotive repair industry through commercial franchising, and specifically targeted small scratches and impacts on vehicles, creating the "Xiaomuzhi" automotive micro-repair system. By 2011, Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company had over 400 franchise stores nationwide. Although "Xiaomuzhi" itself is an existing word, through the continuous use and promotion of its directly operated and franchise stores in the automotive repair field, "Xiaomuzhi" automotive repair has come to identify the business operator and distinguish its services from others in the relevant market. When Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company was established in October 2008, the "Xiaomuzhi" trade name and related services of Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company had already gained a certain degree of market recognition among the relevant public.

2. Whether Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company registered and used the trade name "Xiaomuzhi" with subjective malice. Business operators in market competition should follow the principle of good faith, abide by generally recognized commercial ethics, respect the market labor achievements of others, and when registering an enterprise name, should have the duty to avoid prior trade names in the same industry. In this case, Tianjin Huashang Company, as a franchisee, signed a "Franchise Chain Operation Contract" with Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company, the franchisor of the "Xiaomuzhi" brand, on June 30, 2008. Tian Junshan, the legal representative, signed the contract on behalf of the company, and the company was aware of the relevant contents of the contract. Although Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company claims that it has no connection with Tianjin Huashang Company and that they are two independent legal persons, the legal representatives of both companies are Tian Junshan, and the promotional information and contact information displayed on Tianjin Huashang Company's website directly refer to Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company. Moreover, Tianjin Huashang Company used its registered business location as the business location of Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company's Tianjin main store. Therefore, it should be determined that, as a business operator in the relevant automotive repair market, when Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company was established, it should have been aware of Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company, its business resources, development trends, etc. However, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company still used "Xiaomuzhi" as its trade name, a core identifier distinguishing market entities in the enterprise name, and could not provide a reasonable basis for using "Xiaomuzhi" as its trade name. Subjectively, it clearly had the intention to "free-ride" and to attach itself to the business reputation of others.

3. Whether Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company's use of the trade name "Xiaomuzhi" is sufficient to cause market confusion. According to the facts found, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company, on its website and other promotional materials, prominently highlighted in a special font phrases such as "What to do with small scratches on your car? Find Tianjin Xiaomuzhi" and "Tianjin Xiaomuzhi's professional expertise," and its "discount experience coupons" also stated "For small scratches on your car, find Tianjin Xiaomuzhi." Its target customers largely overlap with the consumer groups of the "Xiaomuzhi" automotive micro-repair system operated by Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company. Furthermore, since 2010, franchise stores of Hangzhou Xiaomuzhi Company in the Tianjin area have been established one after another, and their service areas have also overlapped. Therefore, Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company's registration and use of "Xiaomuzhi" as its trade name inevitably leads the relevant public to mistakenly believe that there is some origin or connection between the two. Coupled with Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company's separate or prominent use of phrases such as "Xiaomuzhi Automotive Repair" and "Tianjin Xiaomuzhi" in its promotions, this is sufficient to cause confusion and misidentification among the relevant public regarding the market entity and the source of services, easily disrupting the order of competition.

Based on the above analysis, the registration and use of this enterprise name by Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company itself violates the principle of good faith, is improper, and regardless of whether it is prominently used, it is difficult to avoid market confusion. This constitutes unfair competition, and Tianjin Xiaomuzhi Company should bear the civil liability to cease using the "Xiaomuzhi" trade name and compensate for corresponding economic losses.

Guiding Case No. 31

Jiangsu Weilun Shipping Co., Ltd. v. Mirana Rosa Company — dispute over damages for ship collision

(Discussed and approved by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on June 23, 2014)

Keywords  
Civil, ship collision, damages, agreement to violate navigation rules, liability determination

Ruling Gist

During navigation, if the vessels involved agree to pass each other in a manner inconsistent with the rules established by the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972, the content of the agreement between the parties and the circumstances under which the vessels involved violated the agreement at the time of the collision shall not be the primary basis for the people's court to determine the liability of the parties. The aforementioned regulations shall still be the criterion, and, on the basis of a comprehensive analysis of the reasons for the formation of the close-quarters situation, the degree of fault of the vessels involved, and the appropriateness of their emergency measures, the liability for the accident shall be determined.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 169 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

On the evening of June 3, 2008, the vessel "Weilun 06" owned by the plaintiff, Jiangsu Weilun Shipping Co., Ltd., and the vessel "MIRANDA ROSE" (hereinafter referred to as the "Rose" vessel) owned by the defendant, Mirana Rosa Company, met in the Yuanyuansha Warning Area of Shanghai Port during their respective voyages. At 23:27 on that day, another foreign vessel "Rio de Janeiro Express," which had departed from the Waigaoqiao Container Terminal, contacted the "Rose" vessel and began to overtake it. At 23:32, the pilot of "Rio de Janeiro Express" called the "Weilun 06" vessel and the "Zheng'an 8" vessel, which was located approximately 0.2 nautical miles ahead to port of "Weilun 06," requesting them to pass green to green. The "Zheng'an 8" vessel refused and made a large starboard turn, quickly crossing to the north side of the warning area and departing. The "Weilun 06" vessel, under the insistence of the pilot of "Rio de Janeiro Express," agreed to pass green to green. The "Rose" vessel then contacted the "Weilun 06" vessel and also requested to pass green to green, and the "Weilun 06" vessel agreed. At 23:38, when the "Weilun 06" vessel reached a position slightly on the starboard bow of the "Rose" vessel, it saw the "Rose" vessel displaying a red sidelight. It immediately contacted the "Rose" vessel and requested it to adjust its course to port as soon as possible. The "Weilun 06" vessel then began to reduce speed, but the "Rose" vessel, because the overtaking vessel "Rio de Janeiro Express" had not yet passed and cleared, and was too close, could not adjust its course to port. At 23:41, the "Weilun 06" vessel passed at close range with the "Rio de Janeiro Express" vessel, now located just ahead to port of the "Rose" vessel, at a distance of only 0.2 nautical miles. At this time, both the "Weilun 06" and "Rose" vessels sensed danger and simultaneously made large port turns. At 23:42, the starboard quarter of the "Weilun 06" vessel collided with the starboard side of the bow of the "Rose" vessel. The accident caused the plaintiff to suffer losses including salvage fees, pollution cleanup fees, cargo depreciation fees, repair fees, and other expenses totaling RMB 4,504,605.75.

The plaintiff then sued the court, alleging that the "Rose" vessel violated the "green to green passing" agreement between the two vessels, and sought an order that the "Rose" vessel bear 80% of the liability. The defendant, on the other hand, argued that the plaintiff should bear 90% of the liability for the collision accident and that some of the losses claimed by the plaintiff were unreasonable.

Judgment

The Shanghai Maritime Court rendered a civil judgment on September 20, 2011, in case No. (2010) Hu Haifa Haichu Zi No. 24: 1. The defendant, Mirana Rosa Company, shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, compensate the plaintiff, Jiangsu Weilun Shipping Co., Ltd., for losses in the amount of RMB 2,252,302.79; 2. The defendant, Mirana Rosa Company, shall, within ten days from the effective date of this judgment, compensate the plaintiff, Jiangsu Weilun Shipping Co., Ltd., for interest on the above amount, calculated at the corresponding period's current deposit interest rate of the People's Bank of China, from June 3, 2008, until the effective date of this judgment; 3. The remaining claims of the plaintiff, Jiangsu Weilun Shipping Co., Ltd., are dismissed. After the judgment was announced, neither party appealed, and the judgment has become legally effective.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held: Before the two vessels reached an agreement, when crossing, they should have passed red to red. The "Rose" vessel, for its own convenience in entering the north channel exit, first proposed a "green to green" passing. This proposal violated the give-way obligation it should have assumed under the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 (hereinafter the COLREGS 1972). However, the "Weilun 06" vessel agreed to this proposal that violated the rules. At that point, the intention of both vessels to pass green to green should mean that throughout the entire avoidance process, both vessels should always show their green sidelights to the other. In this special situation, there were no "give-way vessel" and "stand-on vessel" within the meaning of the COLREGS 1972. Therefore, when a risk of collision arose between the two vessels, both vessels had an equal responsibility to avoid collision, and both should have exercised special caution in accordance with the relevant provisions of the COLREGS 1972. However, in fact, after reaching a mutual agreement to pass green to green, both parties believed that the other would give way to them, failed to effectively observe the conditions of the waters in which they were located and to make a full assessment of the situation and the risk of collision, and did not take action until a close-quarters situation had formed, ultimately failing to avoid the collision. In summary, both vessels were negligent in look-out, failed to use a safe speed, failed to exercise the duty of special caution and take early action to avoid collision, and both violated the provisions of the COLREGS 1972 regarding look-out, safe speed, and action to avoid collision. They bore equivalent responsibility for the occurrence of the collision and should each bear 50% of the liability.

The defendant is the owner of the "Rose" vessel. According to the provisions of the Supreme People's Court's Regulation on Several Issues concerning the Trial of Ship Collision Damage Disputes, the defendant shall bear liability for the losses caused to the plaintiff by the "Rose" vessel in the collision accident. The court determined the specific amount of the plaintiff's losses based on the evidence provided by both parties and, in accordance with the liability share that the defendant should bear, rendered the judgment as above.
